speechtext:
Mr. C. R. McINTOSH (North Battleford) presented the second report of the committee on industrial and international relations, as follows:
Your committee has had before it Bill No. 4. an act to amend the Civil Service Act (Councils), referred to the committee on February 10, 1928. Having considered the bill and examined a number of witnesses on the subject matter involved, your committee beg leave to report as follows:
1.	That whereas the majority of the witnesses heard were of the opinion that further consideration should be given to the details of the constitution of national civil service councils;
C.N.R. Debenture Stock

And whereas the government is prepared to establish such councils;
And whereas the objects of the bill may be attained by order in council;
2.	That this committee endorses the principle of the establishment by the government of a national civil service council, composed of representatives of the government and the organized civil service in equal numbers, to consider and advise the government upon matters of mutual concern to the government and civil servants in their respective capacities as employer and employees, also as to the establishing of any other consultative and advisory machinery that may be required.
3.	That, as the form of constitution for such a council, covering its scope and functions, can best be determined by joint agreement between the parties concerned, this committee recommends the setting up by the government of a drafting committee representing both the government and the civil service organizations, for the said purposes, provided that any such constitutions so drafted shall be subject to the approval of the governor in council; and
4.	That after the said constitution has been drafted and approved in the manner set forth the national civil service council should be established forthwith by the government.
5.	In view of the above recommendations your committee recommend that Bill No. 4 be not further proceeded with.

speechtext:
This time I rise, Mr. Chairman, to support my hon. friend the minister. This is a very old subject. The stock was issued, not to carry interest unless interest was actually earned, but the time is coming when the obligation will have to be met. My hon. friends are perfectly right in meeting it, but in this connection I want to draw one little matter to the attention of the committee. The longer these things run generally the more people want, and I very well recollect, when in 1926 authority was given for negotiations to be entered into with the bankers through whom the business had been handled, the indignation of my hon. friends opposite on returning to office and the manner in which they cancelled

National Health and Veterans' Welfare
the arrangement that had been effected. Now, this is what actually did happen. The first offer was on the basis of the 40-year stock and carried interest at 4i per cent. That interest was not to start to run until May 6, 1930. The governing rate of interest in the market at that time-and I give my hon. friend, not my figures, but the figures of the gentlemen who were dealing with this matter and recommending it to their clients-was 4rJ per cent The discount value of those securities was on that basis, that is, the difference between 4i per cent and 4f per cent, or 93.42. But the securities had to run along from 1926 to 1930 without bearing any interest at all; so a further discount had to be made, which reduced the sum of money which the shareholders would receive under the arrangement to 80. Well, they have every reason to be pleased that my hon. friends stopped the arrangement, because it simply means that today they are getting a million and a half dollars more. The offer which we are now considering is a cash offer which becomes quickly payable. But the only fair way to arrive at its value would be to assume that it was made at the same time as the former offer and to apply the same discounts. Applying those same discounts-and that is going to the very furthest point in case of the proposition-this cash offer would be reduced, so that the value on the market at that time would be only 86, or six points above the offer which my hon. friend cancelled. In other words, it represents on the whole twenty-five million dollars an increase of a million and a half. I am not saying that it will cost the country an extra one and a half million dollars, I am merely pointing out the fact that the shareholders get that much more. It may not cost the country that much more. Why? Simply because the rate of interest in the meantime has gone down. We cannot 6ay exactly what the rate will be, for it depends entirely upon the American market, as we weTe told in the banking and commerce committee by the department's representative who in giving evidence on this question of the rate of interest chargeable by the government under the legislation of 1914 said that it was reduced from time to time having regard to the rate of interest charged in New York. None of us can say exactly what that will be, but it does show clearly that the former settlement was proper, that the liability was a real liability-everybody knew it-and that the shareholders as a matter of fact are getting, as I say, one and a half million dollars more than they would have received under the former arrangement, and their circular shows it.

In connection with this vote for the river St. Lawrence ship channel, and in order that the minister may prepare himself somewhat for the discussion on the estimates for the ensuing year, I wish to call the attention of the committee to certain facts in regard to navigation through the ship channel of the St. Lawrence river. When the later work was undertaken some time ago, it was the intention of the government, as stated, to make a depth of 35 feet for navigation up to and into the harbour of Montreal. From the engineering reports which are now available, it appears that the prevailing levels in Montreal harbour are now about three feet lower than they were at the time when the datum was established for the 35 foot depth. This lowering of the water level in the Montreal harbour is alleged to be due largely to the diversion of water through the Chicago drainage canal, to some extent to a decrease in run-off, and to the channel dredging at various points which facilitates the more rapid flow of the river. If there is a decrease in depth of three feet in comparison with the datum fixed at the time this work was projected, and if the dredging of the river facilitates a more rapid flow of the water, it would appear that the expenditure which we are making on the development of that river is not resulting in the advantages which were estimated at the time this later project was undertaken.

So the reduced depth in the river means a, very great loss indeed to the shipping companies, and also to the traders and merchants of Montreal who are compelled to pay a higher freight rate when ships are not able to take a full cargo.
This 35-foot channel which we are projecting will not be, under present conditions, a 35-foot channel at all. Furthermore, I notice in their report that the engineers, who have been studying the development of the navigation on the St. Lawrence river and Great Lakes, suggest that compensating works should be provided in lakes Ontario and Erie and at other places to restore the levels of lakes Michigan and Huron, and lakes Erie and Ontario further down, which have been lowered by the diversions already made at Chicago and elsewhere. Engineers with whom I have come in contact, who are not partisans of one scheme or another, but who have studied this question, advise me that the construction of these so-called compensating works as proposed, either in connection with the levels of lakes Michigan and Huron or the levels of lakes Erie and Ontario lower down, will still further tend to decrease the depth of water in the harbour of Montreal bo the construction of these compensating works further west will tend to decrease the depth of water actually available for navigation at those seasons of the year when a certain depth is requisite for the shipping of Montreal. Therefore I sugest that when we come to deai with the main estimates in which there is an extra appropriation of something like $1,000,000 under item 220 for the construction and regulating of retaining dams m the St. Lawrence river, and a further appropriation under item 216 of $373,000 for the maintenance and operation of a dredging fleet

we should have a full and complete statement from the minister regarding the works which are now in progress, the extent to which the government proposes to carry on these works, the result with respect to the depth of water available for navigation in the harbour of Montreal and in the river, and some evidence, if it is available, to reassure us that the work of dredging which is being carried on is not actually resulting in further depleting the water which is required in the harbour of Montreal at certain seasons of the year to accommodate shipping which makes its destination there. I do not expect the minister to go into the larger question of the diversion at Chicago w'hich has resulted in such serious loss to Montreal, because I infer that this is a matter which will be dealt with by the Prime Minister or some other member of the cabinet when we are discussing the St. Lawrence navigation scheme which has been suggested by the board of engineers. But I do call the attention of the government as such to the fact that there is an opinion, clearly expressed and apparently well substantiated by the facts, that the projects of compensatory works which have been suggested in connection with the St. Lawrence waterways scheme, the larger scheme will simply result, in robbing Peter to pay Paul: they will diminish the depth avaliable for navigation in the port of Montreal in order to create and retain a greater depth of water in lakes Ontario, Erie, Huron and Michigan. The desire to ascertain the facts-a legitimate desire on the part of those interested in shipping in Montreal-is so great that, I suggest, the minister should prepare himself to give us a clear and definite statement regarding these matters when the estimates for the year are brought down. I do not wish to prolong the discussion on this point, but I thought it wise to call the attention of the minister and of the government to these facts.

The solution of the difficulties suggested by my hon. friend (Mr. Cahan) would seem to me to be a very easy one: if the boats cannot go to Montreal, let them stop at Quebec. For fifty years or more we have been endeavouring to interfere with the course of nature by dredging the channel between Quebec and Montreal. As the hon. member himself says, it is extremely doubtful whether these dredging works have served the purpose which it was sought to attain when the dredging was begun. We have had, first, an agitation for a twenty-five foot channel to Montreal, then for a thirty foot channel and now for one of thirty-five feet. People who understand these things have stated very

Supply-St. Lawrence Ship Channel
definitely that there is a limit to which one can dig in a river such as the St. Lawrence; it is stated that increased dredging tends to allow the water to run off more rapidly than it would otherwise.

The sea will flow
back.

The sea flows back up as far as Quebec, I may tell my hon. friend, and not as far as Montreal. That is one of the natural advantages with which Providence has endowed Quebec. When ships of draught such as mentioned by my hon. friend-ships of thirty and thirty-two feet-are proceeding in a narrow channel with only perhaps from six inches to a foot of water between the keel of the vessel and the bottom, there is a natural tendency to drag from the sides of this narrow channel all the silt and mud and so constantly to refill that portion which has been dredged. This, I think, has been stated by engineers to be one of the reasons why it is almost impossible to maintain a constant depth of thirty-five feet in this channel. Then, owing to the advance of settlement in the upper reaches of the river and the lack of storage facilities always due to vegetation and forests, we find that every spring the water runs off much more rapidly. This is, of course, far more noticeable in the smaller rivers which serve as feeders to the main body, the St. Lawrence river; but the same action is felt in the St. Lawrence also. It is true, perhaps, that the Chicago diversion has had some effect, but generally speaking it will be found, I think, that the principal reason why the St, Lawrence is lower at certain seasons of the year now than it was formerly is that the land has been cleared at the head waters which flow into the river, so that naturally the water flows off much more rapidly.
I had not intended taking part in this discussion, but I want to assure my hon. friend that there is being constructed at Quebec a magnificent port capable of accommodating all the vessels of the type he mentions, and many more, some up to forty feet, and if the hon. gentleman will be prepared to accept, as the lot of the harbour of Montreal, the lot which Providence no doubt intended for it, that of receiving only smaller vessels., and leaving to Quebec the lot of receiving the larger vessels, not asking parliament to intervene in the workings of nature, then possibly we might all get along better.

I have not the slightest objection to the hon. member (Mr. Power) having the mail boats stop at his Indian village, but I want to point out that the depth of
water in the St. Lawrence is a matter of considerable importance to Nova Scotia. We cannot unload, at Quebec, coal from Nova Scotia destined for Montreal; we must get the boats to Montreal.

I do not think any of the small vessels carrying coal-vessels of ten, twelve and fifteen thousand tons-will have any difficulty reaching Montreal. It is the large transatlantic vessels having a draft of twenty-eight and thirty feet which will find it difficult as they have done in the past.

I quite understand that. I may tell the hon. gentleman that I have landed from ocean liners at Quebec and I have also gone up to Montreal on liners and on coal boats. The difference in cost between transporting coal in vessels of eight and ten thousand tons capacity and in vessels of twenty thousand tons is very material.

Are there any vessels of
twenty thousand tons transporting coal from Nova Scotia to Montreal at the present time?

No, but there ought to
be. Before boats of that size will be constructed for the trade the people who will have to operate the boats must know that the required water will be provided and maintained. We have coal boats to-day of 27 and 28 feet draft, and even they are in trouble. I wish to point out to the house that this is not entirely a matter of providing water for the mail boats; there are other interests involved, the only advantage we in Nova Scotia receive from the whole St. Lawrence scheme of navigation is the opportunity to send our coal to Montreal. Hon. members must not think that the city of Quebec and the city of Montreal are the only places interested in the navigation of the upper reaches of the St. Lawrence river.

Will the minister
explain whether this amount is for the general dredging fund or if it is ear-marked for any particular object, because there is a certain section of this country even above Quebec and Montreal which is interested in the development of the St. Lawrence.

This amount is intended
for the general work of deepening the St. Lawrence channel, and in part it is necessary at present because we have increased the salaries of the men working on the dredges and tugs connected with this work. Last year we provided for an increase to a certain class of navigators employed on what we call the Dominion steamers, those ships which are used for the maintenance of the lighthouses,

but having made that increase which was provided for in the main estimates we thought it would be only fair and just to extend it to all the men working on the dredges and tugs which are used in this work.

They account for $100,000 In addition, certain units of the fleet required extensive and unexpected overhauls during the year, which necessitated further unforeseen expenditures approximating $300,000, which this proposed supplementary appropriation covers.
In connection with the main point raised by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, speaking offhand I might say that the engineers of the department in charge of the work are under the impression that we can deepen the channel of the St. Lawrence river profitably for some time to come; we have not reached the point as yet where dredging ceases to be profiable. We can deepen the channel to 35 feet without seriously interfering with the water in the port of Montreal and without causing a greater or more rapid flow of the water in the river. As a matter of fact, the first program which was undertaken to deepen the channel to 30 feet is practically completed, and in the course of probably seven years we will have the channel 35 feet deep from Montreal down. I might emphasize that fact, that the engineers state that we can dredge the channel to a depth of 35 feet without interfering with the water in the port of Montreal. I am not quite clear on the matter, but it seems to me that the deepening of the water in the port of Montreal is a matter under the control of the Montreal harbour commission rather than the Department of Marine and Fisheries. I am not quite sure, but that is my impression at present. In the main estimates to which my hon. friend has referred we are providing for an expenditure of about $1,000,000 for the construction of submerged dams below Montreal, with a view to raising the water in that port and removing the necessity for further dredging. The engineers have reported that if we could construct two or three submerged dams, one below Montreal and one in the vicinity of lake St. Peter, we would raise the level of the water in the port of Montreal by nearly two feet. Of course, when we come to the discussion of the main estimates I will be in a position to give all these details which have been asked for by my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George.
With regard to the safety of navigation between Quebec and Montreal, I may say
[Mr. Cardin-1
that navigation on that section of the river is quite as safe as navigation from Quebec down to the gulf, and in fact the accidents are not so numerous in the section of the river from Quebec to Montreal as they are from Montreal down to the gulf. The channel is very safe, and I have said before that the insurance people are not fair with regard to the St. Lawrence route. I maintain that the rates are too high, because the risks are no greater on the St. Lawrence river than on any other water course in the world. The government of Canada have spent large sums to establish buoys and lighthouses on this route, and I am sure it was a source of great comfort to the Canadian people when a high officer of the American government stated last year that the St. Lawrence route was the best inland route existing in the world. I think the money spent in deepening the St. Lawrence as much as can be done profitably is a wise expenditure, because up to the present navigation on that river has proven very beneficial to the country at large. It has helped develop one of the greatest ports in the world, and the benefits which have been derived by Montreal and by the whole country will amply justify the expenditure which has been made in that connection.
As far as the refilling is concerned, there is none to speak of. The nature of the soil which composes the bed of the river is such that when the dredging is done practically no refilling takes place, and the money we are expending now in deepening that channel is amply justified by the benefits which have been derived.
Then the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George referred to the lowering of the water by three feet in the port of Montreal. I am not prepared to agree that that is the situation. If my memory serves me right, certain engineers have contended that the diversion at Chicago does not very much affect Montreal. It may be affected in some way but at the most it will be a matter of a very few inches That, however, is a matter which is not quite clear, and there are expert opinions on both sides. At all events, may I repeat that I will be very glad to gather all the information in the department and give it to my hon. friend and to the house when we come to the main estimates.

what was probably a slip on the part of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. He made perhaps somewhat invidious comparisons between the casualty rate of vessels below and above Quebec. In that connection

I would simply say that if anything happens to the vessels below Quebec it is not due to a lack of water in the channel, and there never has been any complaint that it was impossible to load vessels at Quebec to their full capacity. I am not a navigator on this occasion. Possibly as neither of us is an engineer or a navigator both our theories may be wrong. The passage of the vessel through the mud and silt is of a nature to draw those materials from the sides into the centre of the channel, particularly in places where the channel is so very narrow that sometimes two or three ships cannot pass abreast.

This is a bill to incorporate a public service company; it does not incorporate an ordinary trading company, and in respect of every public service or public utility company of this character, coming before the house I insist upon my right as a member of this house to ensure, so far as my voice and my vote may do so, that it shall be organized on a cash basis, and that it shall not be a company which may be watered to any extent which may be desired by the promoters. I think the time has come in this country when we are bound to adopt such a policy as that.
I can remember in earlier years when we had to cross the rivers by floats or by ordinary ferries-and when, in order to secure a bridge, the people were prepared to endorse almost any measure and to make almost any concession to the promoters of such a public utility. In the condition in which we find ourselves to-day, however, where a public utility of this character has its success assured from the very start, it should be organized on the basis that the capital of the company shall be paid up in cash, or, if property is to be transferred, that the transfer shall be made at the actual cash value of that property.

Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge
There is no reason in the world why the promoters of this bill need or should be authorized to transfer to the company a single bit of property in payment of its shares. They should subscribe the capital of the company and that capital should be paid up as it is required; they should use that capital when it is paid up to acquire only such property as is necessary to carry out the undertaking which they have in view. The tolls of the company should be subject to the control of the governor in council, as is the case in the present instance, as the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon) pointed out in a previous discussion. Furthermore, he has given us the assurance that with respect to these tolls the governor in council will exercise its right to refer these matters for decision to the Board of Railway Commissioners which is competent to hear the evidence and revise the tolls from time to time. But these tolls should be based upon the traffic of a company such as this, upon the income of such a company in respect of its capital which has been paid up, either in money or in actual money's worth.
Therefore I say I am in favour of this amendment, first because in respect of every incorporated company, which we now have in the province of Quebec and in respect of every bond issue by a company under the Companies Act, parliament has insisted that the company shall file, with the provincial secretary in the case of a Quebec company and with the Secretary of State of Canada in the case of a company incorporated under the Companies Act of Canada, a contract showing how, to what extent and for what consideration every share issued has been paid, if paid otherwise than in cash. That enables the government, by a reference to the Secretary of State, to know exactly on what financial basis the company is organized, and it enables any other person interested to ascertain the same fact in the same way. Therefore that section of this measure is in accord with the best legislative precedents which have been established by parliament, and those precedents should be adhered to in the present case.
Then take the next point. The contract should be filed, and if property must necessarily be acquired by an issue of stock, which I regard as unnecessary and inexpedient in the case of a company of this kind, that property should be acquired at something approximating its real or market value. I have not been objecting at all to the item because I assume that the estimates for this year will go to the special committee, where we shall have an opportunity of going into the manner in which these matters are checked up. But my hon. friend will have to do more than merely certify in gross, and we ought not to have in the future any E. & O. E. statements.
That is right.

The only safe way is not to handle it in gross. There is only one way of doing it, and that is to check it on the billings. The Board of Railway Commissioners have duplicates of all the billings, and there should be no bulk about it at all. The minister ought to have before the committee the officials of the board who are dealing with this question, because it is a very important one.

My hon. friend is quite right respecting the nature of the audit. I would merely ask the committee to remember that the statute came into effect only on the first of July last, and we had to ask the Board of Railway Commissioners to set up the ne-

Supply-Merchant Marine
cessary organization to make the kind of check to which my hon. friend refers. When I said a moment ago that one could look at it in the gross, I did not mean to suggest that the railway commission was using that method, but simply that an idea could be gained by the average individual of what the 20 per cent reduction would amount to if he knew the gross revenue from the movements under review. My hon. friend suggests that the item in the main estimates similar to this might go to the special committee. I really had not thought of sending it there, because it is not a Canadian National Railway item; it is an item under the statute which must be considered in the departmental estimates. If there is any desire to inquire into its application in the specal committee, I shall be very happy to have that done there, but I would not like formally to pick out this item from the departmental estimates and send it to the special committee.

I do not care
how it is done so long as the committee have a chance to find out how the checking is done and that a proper check is kept.
Can the minister give us any information as to whether this 20 per cent reduction has increased the movement of freight in this area?

With the experience we have up to date it has been difficult to answer that question positively. My estimate last year, as my hon. friend pointed out, was about two million and a half dollars, based upon the experience of the then current year. Putting the figures together which we have before us to-night, he will notice that it is running practically in accordance with that estimate. But I must qualify it by the fact that some of the smaller roads did not come under the provisions of the act promptly after July 1. I am informed by maritime members that there is better business down there, which will show us an increase in traffic; but that can only be a general statement. I cannot for a moment give the figures of the tonnage, but I will bear in mind when the main estimates are before the house, when I think possibly I shall be able to give some information in that regard.

Item agreed to.
Amount required to provide for payment to the Canadian National Railway Company of the deficit in receipts and revenues of the eastern lines, as defined in the Maritime Freight Rates Act. occurring within the period July 1, 1927, to December 31, 1927, less the portion of such deficit occurring on account of the application of the said act, $2,117,936.42.
Is this an operating deficit?
Yes.
I am not familiar with the legislation, but I apprehend that this is the operating deficit as the result of the legislation.
This item is not the result of the legislation.
Why is it done in this way?
The legislation provides for its being done this way, but this amount is not the result of the legislation.
My hon. friend has not caught my point. In other words, the legislation did not create this deficit; but the legislation provides for the deficit to be thus reported.	.
That is it.
Does it go to the extent of saying that the deficit is thus to be paid?
Yes.
Then we will have it up twice; we will have it up again in connection with the major statement.
No, it is a receipt in the major account.

We can look
into it just as well in that connection.
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Canadian Government Merchant Marine- Loan to Canadian Government Merchant Marine, Limited, repayable on demand with interest at a rate to be fixed by the governor in council, upon such terms and conditions as the governor in council may determine, and to be applied in payment of:-
Deficits in operation of the company and of the vessels under the company's control during the nine months' period ended December 31, 1927. and working capital requirements, $1,000,00.
I do not think this should be dealt with here at all. It certainly should be referred to the special committee now.

I have an explanation to make in that regard. As my hon. friend states, this is an item which in the ordinary course of events would be referred to the special committee on Canadian National railways and shipping. But the fiscal year of the government ends on March 31. This
175S
Supply-Merchant Marine

estimate was prepared only a day or two ago, has not been before the committee, and cannot get there prior to the end of the fiscal year. I may say that the whole matter of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine will be dealt with by that committee on the main estimates. These we have already tabled. But in connection with this item, the close approach of the end of the fiscal year compels me to present it to the committee of the whole house.
It will be remembered that at the last session no vote was taken for deficit purposes. If my memory serves me correctly, I think there was a vote in the neighbourhood of something like $18,000 for capital requirements, but the showing of the previous year caused the management to believe that possibly they might get along without a deficit during the year 1927. Experience, however, indicates an expected deficit in operation of $559,000. In addition to that there has been a gradual impairment of the working capital from year to year since 1922, in which year the Canadian Government Merchant Marine received from the government working capital to the extent of $930,000. Deficits from time to time have whittled that down until it is now about $84,000-an insufficient amount of working capital. For that reason, and in order to bring the working capital up to the necessities of the business, the balance of this vote of $1,000,000 amounting to $440,000, is asked for.
The condition of the merchant marine during the last few years can be indicated by the following figures: In 1923-24 there was a deficit of $1,829,000,-1 am omitting the odd hundreds-in 1924-25 it was $1,416,000; in 192526, $.595,000; 1926-27, $44,000; and as I indicated a few minutes ago, this year it is estimated to be $559,000.

Will the minister be good enough to tell us how the tonnage compares to-day with that of three or four
years ago?

There has been a steady adjustment in that regard, reviewed by the committee from year to year. Only those ships suitable for the service have been retained, but I cannot give my hon. friend a comparison, for instance, between 1927 and 1926. I can, of course, undertake that everything in that regard will be subject to review by the special committee.
All I am trying to understand is whether the deficit has been reduced by the management getting new markets, or simply because the tonnage has been reduced.

There is no doubt that
the reduction in tonnage has not had any material effect in reducing the deficit, for the ships disposed of were for the most part not in use. In any case where it was found to be impracticable to apply the ships to good business purposes they were in the course of time sold. In general I may tell my hon. friend that I am encouraged by the progress which is being made in this connection. It is needless for me at this time to go into the experience of other countries in this regard; it does not do us much good to take comfort from the sorrows of others; but it is a fact that while our government-owned mercantile marine is not entirely a bonanza, it is at least doing a great deal better than any similarly owned mercantile marine that I know of. And it is performing a real service in connection with Canada's trade, a service which I hope will increase as time goes on.

Has there been
any change in the working year of the merchant marine?
We are this year changing it to the calendar year.
I thought it was always so.
No.

Mr. Chairman, this vote of one million dollars is apparently to cover a deficit for nine months' operation, and if you add to that another 25 per cent you have a very large deficit. I am confining myself strictly to the freight boats which are being operated by the government and am not referring at all to the West Indies services, the new ships for those services not yet being in operation. Let me say at the outset that the criticism of the leading shipping paper in the world, Fair Play of England-I am sorry I have not a copy under my hand- without being able carefully to analyze the accounts, tells a totally different tale from that which is put forward by the government. With regard to these boats, I make the following statement without fear of contradiction, and if I am contradicted I am perfectly willing to submit the matter to any firm of experienced shipping auditors or chartered accountants in the bid country who are familiar with this business. I say that the Canadian merchant marine, if wound up to-day, would be found to have cost the country $125,000,000. And what are the ships doing? To-day they are operating in competition with privately owned ships in every quarter of the globe, going east and west and north and south.

Supply-Merchant Marine
They are competing with privately owned English shipping concerns who are thoroughly familiar with the operation of steamships, and these concerns are paying, as the merchant marine boats are not. The government merchant marine steamers are carrying cargo from the east to various American ports and cutting rates in opposition to the established lines. What are they doing with regard to the Australian, the South African and the New Zealand trade? There are private companies that have been operating in those waters for years, and in comes the merchant marine and cuts rates, to which it has not agreed. The merchant marine is running voyage after voyage at an absolute loss, and I maintain, as I have always done, that the government operation of steamers cannot be profitable. I contend, therefore, that the sooner the operation of the merchant marine is discontinued the better it will be for the taxpayers of the country, who will have less to pay.

I shall appreciate it if
my hon. friend will let me have that criticism of the accounts to which he refers in order that we may submit it to the management and have them appear before the special committee prepared to deal with that criticism, thus enabling the members of the committee, and the house later on if necessary to ascertain the facts, whatever they may be. With regard to the cost to the country, which my hon. friend says would be something in the neighbourhood of $125,000,000 if the merchant marine were wound up now, I do not want to revive the acrimony of past debates in that connection. I am endeavouring to deal as well as I can with the merchant marine as this government found it and as it has since been carried on by the management of the Canadian National Railways. The major portion of the loss certainly cannot be said to be chargeable to the present management of the merchant marine. I prefer to remain on a business plane in discussing the question and not to go back to the origin of the merchant marine, discussing what we have been compelled to do with it. Such a debate might involve a good deal of argument, some of it acrimonious, which would get us nowhere. The country knows perfectly well that we have the ships. They were built under war conditions, as similar ships were built, and while I may have quarrelled with the policy at the time, I do not think that this is the time to discuss that policy or to exchange recriminations regarding it. We are dealing with the conditions that now exist. I do not think that
the Canadian people would be satisfied to have their government owned ships disposed of at the present time, and I will state why. The people of Canada, rightly or wrongly, now own a great railway transportation system and the operation of shipping in connection with that system is a very important factor indeed. The chief competitor of our Canadian National Railway system, the Canadian Pacific Railway, has gone very extensively into the shipping business-extensively and,
I believe, successfully. At any rate the shipping controlled both by the Canadian Pacific Railway and by the Canadian National system is to-day a valuable contributor to the traffic of the railways operated by these two companies, and I do not think there is immediately before us the prospect of completely closing out the merchant marine. We are providing, not through the government merchant marine, it is true, but by special legislation, for the management of the Canadian National Railways to operate a Canada-West Indies steamship service which will, of course, form a part of the same general shipping arrangement which contributes to the success of our railways. I do agree, however, that we should scrutinize with the utmost care this institution which belongs to us and which is operated by the Canadian National railway system; and, I repeat, l shall be very much pleased, as the government will be, to have any criticism either of the presentation of accounts or of the system itself in time to permit us to put it before the management and ask them to appear before the special committee prepared to deal with it thoroughly and in detail. *

No doubt it is
pleasing to the house to hear of the wonderful traffic which the merchant marine is bringing to the railways, but I would ask the minister this question: If these ships are withdrawn does he think the traffic will lose at all? I maintain that private interests would bring m a good deal more traffic because, by reason of the fact that the merchant marine is operating in competition with them, private shipping companies are not favouring our railways. I say, therefore, that the minister would get just as much traffic if not more from the private companies. My judgment, based on observation, is that the merchant marine does not increase the traffic of the railways.

That is, of course, a
matter of opinion which could not be determined by actual test. I am sorry I cannot agree with my hon. friend.
Supply-Merchant Marine

There is evidently one
branch of the service which is not contributing much to the Canadian roads, and that is the service operating from Australia and New Zealand direct to New York. It is not contributing to the building up of traffic on our railways.

Is my hon. friend quite
sure of his facts?

I think so. I understand that the boats from the far east, from Australia and New Zealand, are carrying cargo through the Panama canal and unloading at New York before coming up to Canadian ports. After discharging the bulk of their cargo at Boston or Philadelphia or New York they then come to Canadian ports.
We read in every newspaper of the movement of ships from South Africa, Australia and New Zealand to New York, where they discharge; they do not land here first.

That may be so, and I
suggest to my hon. friends that they examine the management before the special committee as to the reason why these boats from the far east call at American ports, if they do. I have no personal knowledge of it but I know that my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Black) studies these matters and presumably he knows whereof he speaks. But I also presume that the management will have some pretty good business reasons to offer as to why the boats make these calls, if they do.

When the special committee reassembles after the Easter recess the minister might have the management submit a statement regarding the voyages of the various ships. Such a statement should be easily compiled. The complaint which my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Cantley) has voiced I have also heard frequently, that is, that the "Canadian government marine ships operate fcetween two foreign ports and not directly ^between Canadian ports and other parts of the world. I may remind the minister that the Canadian people and this parliament, in so far as it sanctioned the original construction of the ships, had in mind the utilization of the merchant marine for the development of Canadian trade. That was really the only justification for the policy, and any departure from that policy ought to be fully explained and defended, if it can be, by the management before the special committee. This, I suggest, could best be done by having submitted to the committee a report showing the various voyages during the last year at least.
fMr. Dunnin*.]

I will undertake that
that information will be placed before the special committee when these matters are under discussion, as well as any other information which may help the committee to get an understanding of the whole situation. I think we should look into it very clearly.
3ir HENRY DRAYTON: My hon. friend snould do more than that; there is not much use looking into it when it has been done. There is a real business reason why he should get these other amounts through and get that indebtedness out of the way, but of this vote $441,000 is for new capital. Why treat that as last year's business? You want that capital for the future, and my hon. friend would be well advised to let this whole item go to the committee. Certainly there is no excuse for trying to crowd the item through; this is merely a government subsidiary and there is no business reason for hurrying payment of that $559,000. That, can be borrowed, so I would suggest that since we have let these other items go through the minister should take this item and send it to the committee.

I should like to meet my hon. friend on that, but I would point out that the item is properly in the supplementary estimates for the current fiscal year. It relates to the last fiscal year of the merchant marine, and certainly should be payable to them out of money available in this fiscal year. The money has been borrowed and is chargeable in their accounts in that way, and I would ask my hon. friend to reconsider his request.

As my hon.
friend knows, the supplementary estimates are often passed months after the fiscal year is ended, so there can be no trouble about that. If anyone would be hurt it would be different, but this will not injure anyone; it is merely a matter of bookkeeping.

I am afraid no one would be helped either, because I would have to come back with a supplementary item identical to this, and even though I brought it in during the new fiscal year it would remain a supplementary for this year.
Send this one item to the committee.
That would mean the introduction of another supply bill at a later date for 1927-28. I suggest to my hon. friend that it would be an unnecessary complication.

As I see it, the committee should know everything about this

Supply-Merchant Marine
new capital. I am willing to take my hon. friend's word for it now that he has had a loss which he knows nothing about and which he did not think would occur; we will take his word for that at once, but at the same time he says they need something which they have been getting along very well without for some considerable time, and they need it as a supplement to the past year. What has new working capital to do with the past year?
It has been borrowed.
Whose overdraft was that?
The Canadian Government Merchant Marine.

If the Canadian
Government Merchant Marine have already borrowed it from the bank willy-nilly, so far as we are concerned it makes no difference whether it goes over or not. The bank can afford to let it stand out a little while.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I appeal to my hon. friend to allow this item to go through on the assurance of my colleague that the fullest inquiry will be made when it comes before the committee with the other items? I should like to get this properly cleared up before the end of this fiscal year, for one reason, and for another reason the bills are now all printed and ready.

If my hon.
friend tells me that it will help him in his work I am quite satisfied, so long as it is thoroughly understood that we still have a string on the item.
Absolutely.

Will the minister tell
us how many of the boats are laid up, and where they are laid up?
I am compelled to speak without definite information, but I know of only one which is laid up. The Canadian Raider is laid up at Port Burwell.

Before the item passes would the minister tell me if a supplementary estimate is the place where he is going to put items 405 and 406 from year to year? I think there was some conversation about it which I could not hear, but under the statute I believe these should go in the railway estimates.

It is not the intention
in future years to bring in supplementary estimates for items 405 and 406. These will appear as items in the main estimates of the Department of Railways and Canals in accordance with the statute, which I will cite to my hon. friend. With regard to other companies section 9 applies, but with regard to the Canadian National Railways the statute states that in the event of any deficit occurring in any railway fiscal year in respect of the eastern lines, the amount of such deficit shall be included in a separate item in the estimates submitted to parliament for or on behalf of the Canadian National Railways at the first session of parliament thereafter. Now I have my hon. friend's point, which I did not see before. I was very anxious, and the government were very anxious, to present to parliament the whole picture in connection with the Maritime Freight Rates Act, and the manner in which it was working. Consequently that is all placed on one page in .this fashion, and I think it would be well to continue that practice in future estimates, while it is not the intention to bring these items down in the form of supplementary estimates. I would point out that in a certain sense the wording of this estimate does amend the statute, because the statute intends to have the full year expire, then to have an audit take place, after which the railway commission certifies to the result. By following that practice the railway companies are out that amount of money for a considerable period of time, while by introducing an estimate worded in this fashion it will be possible to make payment by the government closer to the time at which the expenditure is incurred by the railways. That is the objective in view.

I am not questioning the
desirability of doing that; I am only pointing out that it is not according to the statute which was passed last year, and I suggest that the procedure be definitely decided upon. Perhaps you will amend the statute, but I am simply pointing out that it should be done in order.

There is nothing of this
nature in the main estimates for this year, so far as I can see.

The railway estimates
are not in the main estimates; they were tabled to-day as a separate estimate.

We do not regard the
Canadian Raider as lost.
Is it damaged?

Yes.

Sickness and Accident Insurance

Have you any
estimate of the damage?
It will be taken care of by that famous insurance fund but there seems to be a good deal of hope that it will not be lost.

Item agreed to.

I do not think there is
any need to detain the committee at any length in regard to this item, as the matter has been pretty clearly placed before the minister. I have but one suggestion to make, if the minister would give it consideration, namely, inasmuch as the one company-and there is only one company of this kind in Canada-has on hand necessarily a large quantity of raw material, I understand something like 12,000 cords of hardwood, some consideration might be given as to the time when this would come into force and effect, say a year, or something of that character. Customs tariff-526. Household blankets wholly of cotton, not to include horse blankets, automobile or steamer rugs, nor similar articles: British preferential tariff, 15 per cent; intermediate tariff, 22J per cent; general tariff, 27J per cent.

I wish to say a word in connection with the tariff in general. The other night, when we were discussing this question in the house, we were assured that the tariff was given to the manufacturers in order to afford some protection to labour employed in industry. I said that if such were the case we in this corner of the house could have a certain amount of sympathy for protection. On looking at the papers this evening I find that the workers employed in one of the most highly protected industries in this country are out on strike because they have had three reductions in pay in the past six months.
I am now referring to the automobile industry. Men employed in the automobile industry at Oshawa are out on strike because some of them have refused to accept a further cut in their wages. If such be the case, the whole idea on which protection io based falls to the ground. I suggest to the minister, in view of the protection that parliament gives to the automobile industry and of the fact that, automobile manufacturers in Canada are continually reducing the wages of men employed in that industry, lowering the standard of their living, and compelling them, in the case I have mentioned, to go out on strike within the past day or two. that the house should take some action in the matter and refuse to continue to give to such industries the protection we have been giving them.

I do not think my hon. friend has proved his case by what he has said. If I remember rightly, there was a reduction in the protection on this very article not long ago which I might with just as much confidence put forward as an argument why they had to reduce wages, but I do not know anything, nor does my hon. friend, about what the circumstances in that particular factory are. I have a great deal of sympathy with what he says about wages, whether in that particular industry or in any other. My contention is-I am not going to argue it now, but it is well supported- that the great thing that will go-I hate to repeat words that I have already uttered- towards the making of security in industrial life and to the fixing of a living wage is this very factor of protection. It is an agent of great potency in producing that particular result. That is the general statement I make,
1764	COMMONS
Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
but I do not attempt to bolster it up by any reference to the industry which my hon. friend mentions, nor do I think that his reference to that industry proves the other side of the case. If there is any way in which we can, by means of the tariff or otherwise, protect the worker more than he is protected now in his security of employment, I am all for doing anything that would help to bring that about.

Anyone who has followed industrial conditions in England during the
last few years since the war realizes that practically the only industries in England which are at all successful to-day, both from the point of view of the industry itself and of the workers engaged in it, are those to which England has given the safeguarding of industries protection, which amounts to 33J per cent. Just a day or so ago I was reading an article in the National Review which I have on my desk upstairs, written by an English manufacturer of the cheaper types of china, and he points out that previous to the war he was selling this crockery throughout the whole world. He had his own market in England, he had the Australian, the South American and the Indian market. Because of the low cost of manufacturing in England he was able to maintain his place in these markets, but to-day, because of the low wages being paid in Czechoslovakia, Germany, Japan, and a number of other countries in comparison with those paid in free trade England he cannot even compete in his own market in England; he has lost altogether the Australian, the Indian and the South American market, and the only hope for his industry to continue and give work to the people engaged in it and afford him a chance to succeed is that it shall receive, as other industries have received, the safeguarding of industries protection. I say with the utmost respect for the opinion of my hon. friend (Mr. Heaps), because I am quite sure he is sincere in his support of the workingman, that anyone who gives this question any thought must realize that the goods produced in the countries of Europe that have lower standards of living and lower wage scales must to a certain extent be kept out of those countries where higher wages and better standards of living prevail if the industries in those latter countries are to compete. Look over the different industries of England to-day and you will find that practically the only ones that are successful are those that are receiving the 33J per cent protection under the Safeguarding of Industries Act, and they are the only

ones that are able to compete in the markets of the world because of the lower wages and lower standards of living prevailing in other countries.

I would point out to the hon. member that one of the highest protected countries in the world is Japan, and not only has it a high protective tariff, but a 200 per cent anti-dumping law which is put into effect against American goods.
But it is one of the lower standard of living countries.

That merely goes to prove
that protection does not of necessity raise the standard of living, or it would be high in Japan. What we have to contend with in this country in the automobile' business is the competition not of Japan or of 'Czechoslovakia but of the United States, where wages are higher than they are in Canada. The point I raised was that when parliament gives great concessions to certain industries and protects them the way it does, those industries owe something to the workers employed in them. But what protection has General Motors of Oshawa given to the men employed in that industry? Two years ago they treated their employees in a very miserable way. They got them to come to Ottawa in a huge delegation, and when I moved amongst these men I found that hardly any of them knew why they had come here. Parliament gives to that industry a protection which is worth a great deal to the industry, and that being the case the industry owes something to the men and women engaged in it. But what has happened? We find by this evening's paper the men have had two cuts in wages, and they refuse to accept a third. The wages they are receiving now are lower than are being paid in the same industry in the United States. When they were here these men told me' that they were working under conditions that were far from the best, that they were receiving from 42J to 75 cents an hour, the1 average being not much over 50 cents an hour-considerably below a living wage; yet the stock of that company, because of the flourishing condition of the industry, attributable in some degree to the high protection it enjoys to-day, is now over 200, and it may be worth only one-tenth of that.
You are speaking now of General Motors in the United States.

The Oshawa company is a subsidiary, and it also is enjoying a great deal of prosperity, as is manifested by the additions it has made to its buildings at

Ways and Means-Customs Tariff
Oshawa in the last few months. Why should parliament protect an industry of that character? If we have any lever to use over such an industry, I say that it should be used when they are taking away from the workers something which they have no right at all to take away. The question of what is happening in other countries, the tariffs of Czechoslovakia, Australia and Japan, do not enter into this question at all. This is a question of one particular industry in Canada which is enjoying a high degree of protection, the gift of this parliament, yet it takes that gift to further its own interest at the expense of its employees. If that is the case I believe parliament would be justified at the very first opportunity in expressing its strong disapproval of the action which the management of that company has taken toward the men it employs.

I just wish to say that I was not arguing in regard to that particular case at all. The hon. gentleman when he was speaking previously had said that if this is the way the Oshawa industry is treating its employees, all that argument about protection protecting the working man is wiped out. It was a general argument I was making. I was not speaking of this particular case because I have a great deal of sympathy with the remarks of the hon. gentleman in that regard. I was speaking of protection in general.

It does seem to me that those people who'pretend to represent labour in this house have a very meagre knowledge of the requirements of labour in this country. There is no question at all that what this country wants to-day is work. AH you have to do is to survey the industries of thia country, and find out where that work can be got. I would ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Heaps) what he would do if all the industries of this country were closed down. Where would labour go then? Does he want a still bigger army marching across the border into the American republic to get work in one of the highest protected countries in the world? That is what has been happening in this country for a number of years.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. I think we are getting far away from the subject of cotton blankets. I am always glad to hear my hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario because he is so very sincere about everything, and I have no objection to listening to my hon. friends from Winnipeg and Port William, but really this debate is becoming too much enlarged.

I think the hon. member is a little mixed in his point of order. I would tell the hon. member for North Winnipeg that a few years ago hundreds of men were employed in my constituency but to-day their jobs have disappeared.
Mr. Chairman, I should like your ruling on my point of order-that the discussion has wandered far afield from the resolution before the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not think the
hon. gentleman's point is well taken. The hon. member who has the floor is discussing the principle of protection, and the item now before the committee provides for protection of 15, 22J and 271 per cent.

I contend, Mr. Chairman, that if it were not for the principle of protection-which, I admit, is inadequately applied-there would be no work here at all. If the hon. member for North Winnipeg had his policy put into force, our working men would not have any jobs at decent wages.
Why?

Because there would not be any work except for the agricultural classes. What happened a few years ago to our leather industry? Factories were closed, and to-day those workmen are gaining a livelihood in the United States. What happened to the glass industry when the Libby-Owens Company went out of business? Not only did their workmen lose their jobs, but men in the bush were also adversely affected. For instance, in my riding two lumber firms were supplying that company with all their rough lumber for making boxes, and naturally when the glass industry went out of business the men back in the bush lost their jobs. The same can be said of the automobile industry. It is true the government tinkered with the tariff on automobiles two years ago, and then modified their action, but to-day there are five thousand fewer jobs in the automobilp industry^ than there were at that time. Is that the kind of policy the member for North Winnipeg wants to establish in this country? Does he want to destroy completely every chance of our working men getting jobs. I have a great deal of sympathy with him when he advocates raising the working man's wages; but the first thing the Canadian working man wants is a job.

May I ask the hon.
member a question?

Yes, if it is not too hard.

my hon. friend does not know what he is talking about.

My point is that the working men of this country must have jobs, and until they get them our population is not going to increase. Every man who is not a parasite wants to work at a reasonable wage. For the life of me I cannot see how you are going to close down industries and cause unemployment and still keep our working people in the Dominion. You cannot do it, as our experience during the last five years amply proves. The exodus will continue at that rate as long as we pursue our present policy. What protection does primarily is to protect the working man to the extent that it protects his job. If you destroy his job what are you going to do? In my own village industries have been destroyed and their buildings torn down, although for forty years they were employing hundreds of men. Do hon. members think that that is not a serious matter? Are not our working people a national asset? I say again, as long as you pursue this policy that is what will happen. Take the agricultural implement industry: last year we 
imported thirty millions dollars' worth of agricultural implements. If those implements had been manufactured in Canada there would have been work for the people that our friends from Winnipeg are supposed to represent, and do not.
It is not simply a supposition; we do represent Winnipeg.
You think you do.
No, we do. If you think we do not, come to Winnipeg North and Winnipeg North Centre and see for yourself.
North Winnipeg is not the whole Dominion. That is the fault with the members for Winnipeg,-
Neither is Muskoka.

But I think there are many members in this house who represent labour a great deal more accurately than do the members for Winnipeg. Winnipeg, as I said, is not the whole Dominion, and all Canadian labour is not centred there-in fact a very small part of it. On behalf of the labouring people of my riding and of the other ridings that are represented by my colleagues, I want to say that the government is not protecting sufficiently the labouring man's job. There should be greater protection, rather than less. I am not speaking in the interests of the manufacturers, but in the interests of the labouring people. As long as we continue a policy that takes away jobs from our working men and drives them out of the country, then I say the Dominion is worse off to that extent. In to-day's paper I read that Canada and Mexico have been supplying the United States with practically all their immigrants. Within the last six months fifty thousand Canadians have migrated

across the line. How long can this country stand such a drain? We are losing the very best of our native-born, the educated, the ambitious, the industrious. When I am home not a week passes that I have not to make out medical certificates for the very best people in my riding; they are going to the United States. I contend that nothing but an adequate protective policy will provide work and keep our people at home. We have tried everything else more or less. Now give us a fair protective policy for the working men of this country and see what we can do.

Customs tariff-138b. Automobiles for conveying passengers only, n.o.p., valued at retail at place of production, when new, with standard equipment complete at not more than $1,200 each; motor cars or motor trucks (not for railways or tramways) for carrying goods only; motorcycles; chassis for motor vehicles specified in this item:	British preferential
tariff, 124 Per cent; intermediate tariff, 174 per cent; general tariff, 20 per cent.
This is something entirely new; the minister should explain it.

This is designed to correct
what seems to be an unfair discrimination arising out of the legislation of 1926, at which time automobiles valued at $1,200 or less could be imported at 20 per cent whereas cars valued higher than $1,200 were still subject to a duty of 274 per cent. Under the law as it stands, an automobile which is manufactured in Detroit is transported through the
western states on its way to Winnipeg, that being the shortest route. The car might be worth $1,200 in Detroit, or perhaps a little less, but when it enters Winnipeg, for purposes of duty the freight is added, thus bringing it into the class that would pay the .274 per cent duty. In that case there is a discrimination to the extent that the man who imports a car at Windsor has to pay a duty of only 20 per cent as compared with a duty of 274 per cent imposed upon the western Canadian importer. This amendment is intended to remedy that situation. I should add that while this fixes the rate at 20 per cent-because the value of the car for duty purposes is to be taken as at the point of production, say at Detroit-the 20 per cent will be paid on the value plus freight at the point it enters Canada.

The point that strikes me is that this will be a discrimination against the Canadian railways. Previously the man importing the same car at Windsor from Detroit brought it over the Canadian railways and paid 20 per cent, whereas if the car were transported by American railways through Minneapolis and St. Paul to Winnipeg the duty was increased above 20 per cent owing to the extra freight. What the minister is doing is to encourage people in western Canada particularly to import over American railways. It seems to me that this amendment will operate to the profit of the American railways and to the disadvantage of the Canadian roads.

There is some force in what my hon. friend says, and the same thing occurred to me. But if the car came from some distant point inland in the United States and were brought to Windsor the freight would be considerably increased.
That does not apply in the summer when there is traffic by boat, and I am not sure that it is true of the rail haul.
I think the minister is overlooking the fact that there is competition.
It frequently happens that a man wants a car on short notice and he might cross the line from British Columbia, say, to Seattle or Portland.

It is the duty of the customs department to collect revenue and not to direct railway traffic in this country. The railways can be trusted to get their share of the business and it is not for us to use the tariff to force people to ship their goods over one railway instead of another.

Machines and implements for agricultural purposes moved by mechanical power; and motor vehicles, valued at not more than one thousand dollars, and boats for fishing purposes if actually owned abroad by the settler for at least six months before his removal to Canada, and subject to regulations prescribed by the Minister of National Revenue. Is this a concession to people who are coming in or is it an extra burden?

Under the law as it stands, under certain conditions, the effects of settlers coming into Canada are free of duty. That includes automobiles valued at $1,000 or less at present. If the oar is valued at more than $1,000, however, it becomes immediately dutiable for the full amount, so you have this situation: A car valued at $1,000 comes in free, whereas a car valued at $1,050 pays a tax on the entire amount. If it is fair to exempt entirely an automobile valued at $1,0000 or less it seems to me fair to exempt $1,000 of any sum greater than that. This is designed to correct that situation.

Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Income War Tax Act, and to provide:
1.	That the schedule of rates of income tax pertaining to individuals be reduced for the year 1927 and thereof by twenty per centum.

3.	That allowance for exhaustion of mining lands, oil and gas wells and timber limits be afforded to and apportioned between lessee and lessor.
4.	That the income from the operation of ships owned or operated by a non-resident person or corporation be exempt from taxation, provided that the country of residence grants an equivalent exemption in favour of a person or corporation resident in Canada.

0.	That upon election by the trustee controlling a superannuation pension fund or plan to have the investment income exempt from taxation the contributions by employees shall not be exempt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have a rather long memorandum on that. The substantial principle established under the income tax law is that mineral royalties received by the fee owner and the profits made by the operating lessee of the mineral rights above the cost of operation are income. Under the statutory allowance for depletion it cannot be twice credited, Once to the fee owner and once to the lessee; the depletion belongs as of right to the fee owner.
